description: Short-lived Carolingian middle kingdom (843–855) created by the Treaty of Verdun for Lothar I, comprising Italy, Burgundy, Provence, and the Rhine corridor; its rapid fragmentation among Lothar's sons and eventual absorption by East and West Francia proved the impossibility of maintaining a viable middle kingdom between the two dominant Carolingian successors.

temporal.notes: Short-lived; partitioned at Treaty of Meerssen 870

lifecycle_phases.description: The Treaty of Verdun (843) divides the Carolingian Empire among Louis the Pious's three surviving sons: Louis the German gets East Francia, Charles the Bald gets West Francia, and Lothair I gets the middle strip, 'Middle Francia' or Lotharingia, including Italy, Burgundy, Provence, and the Rhine corridor. It is an artificial creation designed to give the eldest (Lothair) the dignity of emperor and Rome. Lothair's son Lothair II rules Lorraine (Lotharingia); his death without legitimate heirs (869) leads to the Treaty of Meerssen (870), dividing Middle Francia between East and West Francia.

Lothair I retains the imperial title alongside Middle Francia, but the title provides symbolic weight without coherent governance. His court at Aachen attempts to maintain Carolingian administrative traditions, but the empire lacks the geographic compactness needed for effective rule across its Italian, Burgundian, and Lotharingian territories.

rise_factors.description: Middle Francia existed solely as a diplomatic compromise at the Treaty of Verdun (843); Lothair I received it as the portion due the eldest son and Holy Roman Emperor, not because of any organic political unity in the territory

Middle Francia was created by the Treaty of Verdun (843) as a compromise to prevent civil war between Louis the Pious's sons; Lothar I received it as the eldest son's share, including the imperial title and the two traditional Carolingian heartlands (Aachen and Rome)

The Rhine and Rhône valleys formed the commercial spine of Middle Francia; control of these river arteries meant control of the most important trade routes between the North Sea and the Mediterranean, giving whoever held them structural economic advantages

As the heir to Charlemagne's imperial title, Middle Francia's rulers possessed the most powerful legitimizing claim in Christendom; the imperial title attracted the allegiance of German bishops, Italian magnates, and border lords who wanted connection to imperial dignity

The Treaty of Verdun (843) created Middle Francia for Lothair I as the eldest Carolingian brother, giving him an elongated realm stretching from the North Sea to central Italy including the imperial capital Aachen and Rome.

decline_factors.description: Lothair II's death without legitimate heirs (869) was the fundamental cause of Middle Francia's dissolution; the Treaty of Meerssen (870) divided the territory between East and West Francia because there was no legitimate heir to inherit it as a unit

Middle Francia was never a coherent political unit; it stretched from the Low Countries to Rome, containing distinct regions (Lorraine, Burgundy, Provence, Italy) with no shared language, culture, or administrative tradition

Lothar I partitioned Middle Francia among his three sons in 855, Louis got Italy, Charles got Provence/Burgundy, Lothar II got Lorraine; this three-way split destroyed the political coherence that had barely held the middle kingdom together and invited East and West Frankish predation

Middle Francia had no natural geographic unity; stretching from Frisia to the Po valley, it lacked the Rhine frontier of East Francia or the Seine basin of West Francia; without a defensible core, it was a collection of territories whose neighbors systematically absorbed them

On Lothair I's death in 855 Middle Francia was divided among his three sons: Louis II received Italy, Charles Provence, and Lothair II got Lotharingia, dismembering the central kingdom that had theoretically balanced east and west.
